slides.title: Roadmap

slides.html:
Gaps and arrival times

  • T_n are i.i.d. exponential with mean 1/\lambda
  • S_n=\sum T_i\sim\Gamma(n,\lambda)
  • Conversely: exponential gaps ⇒ Poisson (handy for simulation)
\{N(t)=n\}=\{S_n\le t<S_{n+1}\}
slides.title: Gaps and arrival times

slides.html:
Time-dependent types

An event at time s is of type i with probability P_i(s):

N_i(t)\ \text{independent Poisson},\quad E[N_i(t)]=\lambda\int_0^tP_i(s)\,ds

M/G/\infty: number in system \to\lambda E[S]; departed and present counts are independent.

Compound Poisson X(t)=\sum_{i\le N(t)}Y_i: mean \lambda tE[Y], variance \lambda tE[Y^2].
slides.title: Time-dependent types

slides.html:
Renewal processes

Gaps X_n i.i.d. (distribution function F), S_n=\sum X_i, N(t)=\sup\{n:S_n\le t\}.

  • N(t)<\infty a.s. and N(\infty)=\infty
  • P\{N(t)=n\}=F_n(t)-F_{n+1}(t) (F_n = n-fold convolution)
  • Borel–Cantelli: \sum P(E_i)<\infty ⇒ only finitely many occur a.s.
slides.title: Renewal processes

slides.html:
Stopping times and Wald

\{N=n\} is determined by X_1,\dots,X_n.

E\Big[\sum_{n=1}^NX_n\Big]=E[X]\,E[N]
  • N(t)+1 is a stopping time; N(t) is not
  • E[S_{N(t)+1}]=\mu\,(m(t)+1)
  • Example: roll a die until the first 6: expected sum 3.5\times6=21
slides.title: Stopping times and Wald

slides.html:
Renewal theorems

Elementary: m(t)/t\to1/\mu

Blackwell: non-lattice m(t+a)-m(t)\to a/\mu; lattice \to d/\mu

Key renewal: \int_0^th(t-x)dm(x)\to\frac1\mu\int_0^\infty h

Limiting residual life: \dfrac1\mu\int_x^\infty(1-F), mean \dfrac{E[X^2]}{2\mu}.
slides.title: Renewal theorems

slides.html:
Renewal equation and rewards

B=h+B*F\ \Rightarrow\ B=h+h*m\ \ (\text{unique locally bounded solution})

Renewal reward:

\frac{R(t)}t\to\frac{E[R]}{E[X]}

Long-run reward rate = mean reward per cycle / mean cycle length.
slides.title: Renewal equation and rewards

slides.html:
Definition and Chapman–Kolmogorov

P\{X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i,\dots,X_0\}=P_{ij}
P^{(n+m)}=P^{(n)}P^{(m)}=P^{n+m},\qquad\pi^{(n)}=\pi^{(0)}P^n

Finite-dimensional laws are determined by the initial law and P.
slides.title: Definition and Chapman–Kolmogorov

slides.html:
Communication and first passage

  • i\to j: \exists n,\ P_{ij}^{(n)}>0; i\leftrightarrow j is an equivalence
  • f_{ij}^{(n)}: first-passage probability; f_{ij}^*=\sum_nf_{ij}^{(n)}
  • P_{ij}^{(n)}=\sum_{l\le n}f_{ij}^{(l)}P_{jj}^{(n-l)}
\sum_{n\ge0}P_{ii}^{(n)}=\frac1{1-f_{ii}^*}
slides.title: Communication and first passage

slides.html:
Recurrence and transience

i recurrent ⇔ f_{ii}^*=1 ⇔ \sum P_{ii}^{(n)}=\infty

i transient ⇔ f_{ii}^*<1 ⇔ \sum P_{ii}^{(n)}<\infty

  • Recurrent and i\to j ⇒ i\leftrightarrow j, j recurrent
  • Positive recurrent \mu_i<\infty; null recurrent \mu_i=\infty
  • Null recurrent ⇔ P_{ii}^{(n)}\to0
slides.title: Recurrence and transience

slides.html:
Stationary law and ergodic theorem

\pi=\pi P,\quad\pi\ge0,\quad\sum\pi_j=1

Irreducible: positive recurrent ⇔ a stationary law exists, and \pi_j=1/\mu_j.

  • Aperiodic: P_{ij}^{(n)}\to\pi_j
  • In general: visit frequency \to\pi_j
  • Detailed balance \pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji} ⇒ stationary

Example: \begin{pmatrix}.7&.3\\.4&.6\end{pmatrix} has \pi=(4/7,3/7).
slides.title: Stationary law and ergodic theorem

slides.html:
Rate matrix and Kolmogorov equations

Sojourn times are exponential; then the chain follows the jump chain.

Q=P'(0),\qquad P'=QP=PQ,\qquad P(t)=e^{tQ}

Stationary law: \pi Q=0. Two states:

P_{00}(t)=\frac b{a+b}+\frac a{a+b}e^{-(a+b)t}
slides.title: Rate matrix and Kolmogorov equations

slides.html:
Common pitfalls

Mistake Correct
Thinned processes are correlated They are independent
The covering interval has mean 1/\lambda About 2/\lambda (inspection paradox)
N(t) is a stopping time N(t)+1 is
m(t)=t/\mu always Only for Poisson; in general m(t)/t\to1/\mu
Recurrent ⇒ positive recurrent The symmetric walk is null recurrent
Periodic chains converge to \pi Only time averages do
slides.title: Common pitfalls
